old: Its name simply counts its wheels and names their shape, in a word stitched together from two borrowed pieces.
The second half comes from a Greek word for "circle," the same root behind the English word cycle.
French built it from bi- meaning "two" plus cycle, before English adopted it in 1868.
clues: This everyday vehicle got its English name from French, where speakers later swapped the original word for a longer version while English kept it unchanged.
A pedal-powered vehicle with two wheels in a line and handlebars for steering; unlike a motorcycle it has no engine, and unlike a tricycle no third wheel.
A skill you never forget, people say, is just like riding one. Its name counts its wheels, and its second half traces to an ancient Greek word for circle.
